related.en: the first coffee, served to a guest
the last coffee, a hint that it's time to go home

note:
Coffee in Serbian is ка̀фа, and it has many playful names for its taste or the occasion:
• чемѐрика - bitter, from че̏ме̄р
• дочекуша - the first one, for a guest, from до̀чекати
• сѝктеруша - the last one, a hint that it's time to go home, from сиктер
• кајмакара - very thick
• шећеруша - sweet
• шлогируша - knockout-strong, from шло̑г
title: Nicknames for coffee

note:
Ћева̀пи and плѐскавица are tourist food, not everyday meals.

At home Serbs more often cook:
• бора̀нија, гра́шак with meat
• па̏прика̄ш, ђу̀веч, са̀тараш
• пуњена паприка, са̀рма, муса̀ка

The fridge usually holds сла̀нина, коба̀сица, па̀влака, си̏р, пѐкмез and паште́та.

The obligatory first course at lunch is су̏па.
title: What Serbs eat at home

note:
Serbian uses one word, навлака, for both a pillowcase and a duvet cover:
• навлака за јастук - a pillowcase, also called ја̀стучница
• навлака за јорган - a duvet cover

Јо̀рган is the duvet itself.
title: Pillowcase and duvet cover

related.en: two-room apartment: a living room and a bedroom
three-room apartment: a living room and two bedrooms
the 1st floor above the ground (US: second floor)
the 2nd floor above the ground (US: third floor)

note:
Listings count rooms by the living space, not the bedrooms:
• једно̀собан - a one-room apartment, like a studio
• дво̀собан - a living room and a bedroom
• тро̀собан - a living room and two bedrooms

Floors are counted from the ground floor:
• при́зе̄мље - the ground floor
• пр̀вӣ спра̏т - the 1st floor above it (US: second floor)
• дру̏гӣ спра̏т - the 2nd floor above it (US: third floor)

Utilities are ре̏жије, rent is кѝрија or стана̀рина.
title: How rooms and floors are counted in rental listings

related.en: to tap eggs against each other

note:
At У̏скрс Serbs tap dyed eggs against each other: two people knock the tips together, and whoever's egg cracks loses.

When visiting, it is customary to bring an egg for the hosts, and the loser gives his egg to the winner.

There are even tournaments, called Туцанијада.

The verb: туцати јајима, туцамо - "we tap eggs".
title: Туцање јајима: egg tapping at Easter

note:
Serbia has no kulich or paskha.

In the morning people eat dyed eggs, ку̏вана шу̑нка, по̀гача, си̏р, ка̀јмак, ку̏лен, мла̑д лу̏к and ро̀тквица. Bread is not taken to church, only the eggs are blessed.

The main dish of the lunch is јагњеће печење, with крофне, орехњача or мако̀вњача and пи̏та са ја̏букама for dessert.
title: The Easter table in Serbia

note:
Пѝринач and сѝрће came from Turkish.

Ко̀зице is the ordinary word for shrimp, literally "little goats". Гамбори is more often heard in Croatia and Slovenia, and шка̏мпи are langoustines with claws.

The other words: јѐгуља, да̏гња, штапићи.
title: Where the words for sushi and seafood come from

note:
The adjective ки̏сео is broader than "sour":
• ки̏селӣ ку̀пус - sauerkraut
• ки̏селӣ кра̏ставац - pickled cucumber
• кисела вода - sparkling mineral water
• кисела киша - acid rain
• ки̏селӣ о̏сме̄х - a forced, insincere smile
title: Кисело: not only a taste

note:
Some words have a masculine and a feminine variant, both equally correct:
• мѝнӯт and мину́та
• сѐкунд and секу̀нда
• ли̏тар and ли̏тра
• палачи́нак and палачи́нка
• ко̀верат and ко̀ве̄рта

Sometimes the difference is one of style or region, but more often there is none, and both variants are heard equally.
title: Words with two genders

note:
The classics for hot weather:
• шпри̏цер - white wine with sparkling or plain water
• сок од зове - a drink made from elderflower syrup
• сок од вишње
• лимуна́да - water with lemon and sugar or honey
• ле̏денӣ ча̏ј, точено пиво

Кисела вода is sparkling water, often with lemon.
title: What people drink in Serbia in summer

note:
In messages people use abbreviations:
• vrv - ве̏рова̄тно
• msm - ми̏слӣм
• nmg - не мо̀гу
• nzm - не зна̑м
• nmj - не̏мој

This is colloquial chat style; it is not used in formal letters.
title: Abbreviations in Serbian chats

note:
From verbs and nouns Serbian forms names of places with the suffix -оница: учио́ница, радио́ница, перѝоница, залагао́ница.

Once you know this suffix, the meaning of a new word can often be guessed.
title: The suffix -оница: a place of action

note:
Serbian has separate words for different kinds of packaging:
• конзѐрва - a tin can: fish, pâté
• лѝме̄нка - a metal can: soda, beer
• те́гла - a glass jar: jam, honey, ajvar
• фла̏ша, ку̀тија, ке̏са, ке̏сица, џа̑к
• ка̀рто̄н - a large box
title: Packaging: can, jar, bag, box

note:
Serbs speak about weight gently:
• бу̏цмаст, буцмаста - affectionate, mostly about babies and chubby cheeks
• пунији, пунија - neutral, about adults who are on the fuller side
• елегантно попуњен (-а) - jokingly refined, implies dignity and style
title: How to say "plump" politely

note:
Ottoman rule left words for daily life, trade and crafts: са̑т, ча̏к, ба̀рем, ћо̀шак, ку́ла, џа́мија, ђу̏бре, ме̏рмер, ѐксер, чѐлик, ба̀кар, за̀на̄т, ма̀рама, џе̏п.

They stuck because they were handy, had no equivalent, and became part of the culture.

Words about food and household items are in the first collection.
title: More Turkisms: everyday words

related.en: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs

note:
Serbian titles are often translated, not copied:
• Пепѐљуга - "Cinderella"
• Снежана и седам патуљака - "Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs"
• Лепо̀тица и зве̑р - "Beauty and the Beast"
• Мала сирена - "The Little Mermaid"
• Кра̑љ ла̏во̄ва̄ - "The Lion King"
• Маза и луња - "Lady and the Tramp"

The last one's title conveys the characters: ма̏за is a pampered favorite, луња is a street tramp.
title: Cartoon titles in Serbian

note:
In autumn Serbia switches to зимско време: the clocks go back an hour, and the time difference with other countries changes.

Useful expressions:
• поме́рати са̑т
• временска разлика
• временска зона

The word вре́ме means both time and weather.
title: Changing the clocks: useful words

related.en: slava, the family's patron saint's day
to a slava, as a guest

note:
Сла̏ва is the Serbian celebration of a family's patron saint (све́тац). On December 19 many people celebrate Ни̏кољдан, St Nicholas' Day.

The family prays and lays a table with bread and fish, because it falls in a fasting period. The slava is celebrated at home, so shopping malls are empty that day.

The greeting is Срећна слава!

A joke: half of Serbia celebrates its slava, the other half goes to a slava as guests.
title: Slava: the family patron saint's day

related.en: the Moscow cake (from a Belgrade hotel)
a sponge cake soaked in three kinds of milk

note:
What to try:
• торта «Мо̏сква» from a Belgrade hotel
• трилече - a sponge cake soaked in three kinds of milk
• бајадѐра, кре̏мпита, урмашице
• сла̀тко̄, ва̀нилице, бакла̀ва, слатка пита

The Moscow cake was invented in Belgrade, not in Russia.
title: Serbian sweets

related.en: the first coffee, for a guest

note:
Coffee in Serbian is ка̀фа. Colloquial speech has invented many nicknames for it, and each one describes the taste or the situation right away:
• чемѐрика - bitter, from че̏ме̄р
• дочекуша - the first one, for a guest, from до̀чекати
• сѝктеруша - the last one, a hint that it's time to go home, from сиктер
• кајмакара - very thick
• шећеруша or шербетуша - sweet
• шлогируша - so strong it nearly gives you a stroke, from шло̑г
title: Playful names for coffee

note:
Serbia is seen as a land of meat eaters, but at home people eat many vegetable and side dishes that are not on tourist menus.

The fridge usually holds сла̀нина, коба̀сица, па̀влака, си̏р, пѐкмез and паште́та.

Favorite home dishes:
• бора̀нија, гра́шак, пѝла̄в
• са̀тараш, па̏прика̄ш, муса̀ка
• пуњена паприка
• са̀рма - New Year is not complete without it

The first course at lunch is almost always су̏па.
title: What Serbs really eat at home

related.en: Serbian coffee brewed in a cezve

note:
The national strong drink is ра̀кија: plum, grape or apricot.

Медо̀вача is a sweet rakija with honey, softer and more aromatic. Шумадијски чај is actually hot rakija with sugar, served in winter.

Among soft drinks, the sparkling mineral water «Кне̑з Мѝлош» is popular.

The most recognizable symbol is домаћа кафа, brewed in a cezve, with a thick foam on top.
title: Serbian drinks

related.en: the red egg, the guardian of the house

note:
On Вѐликӣ пе́так Serbs dye Easter eggs (фарбати јаја), and the first one is always red. It is called чува̀ркућа - "the guardian of the house".

The egg is kept until the next Easter: it is believed to protect the family from misfortune.

When the new Easter comes, the old egg is buried in the ground or given to a river. If there is no river nearby, it is flushed down the toilet with running water.
title: The red egg чуваркућа

note:
Serbia has no kulich or paskha: the word У̏скрс means only the holiday itself.

In the morning people eat dyed eggs, кувана шунка, по̀гача, си̏р, ка̀јмак, пр̀шут, ку̏лен, мла̑д лу̏к and ро̀тквица. Bread is not taken to church: after the liturgy only the eggs are blessed.

Lunch is roast ја̏гње and appetizers (пре̏дјело), with крофне, пи̏та са ја̏букама and мако̀вњача for dessert.

The family gathers at one table, all generations together.
title: The Easter table in Serbia

related.en: cheekbone; fingertip pad; a little strawberry

note:
Ја̏года in Serbian means only a strawberry. Berries in general are called бобичасто воће, literally "berry fruit".

Summer at the market:
• ја̏года, ма̀лина, боро́вница
• ку̀пина, ри̏бӣзла
• тре̏шња, ви̏шња, гро̑жђе

Јаго̀дица is the cheekbone, the pad of a finger, and also a "little strawberry".
title: Berries: јагода means strawberry

note:
The basic word for "money" is но̀вац, and па̏ре comes second. Both fit everywhere except official documents.

Cash: ке̏ш, готовѝна. Tip: ба̀кшиш.

Slang: ло́ва, ки̑нта, ди̏нџа. Ки̑нта comes from the Albanian qindarkë, a small coin.

Examples: пу̏н је па̏ра, дугујеш ми кинту, нисам при кинти.
title: Money in Serbian: from novac to kinta

note:
Many animals have their own word for the young, and it is neuter: штѐне, ма̏че, тѐле, ждре̑бе, ја̏гње, ја̏ре, пра̑се, пи̏ле, па̏че, ла̏не, ме̏че.

Don't mix up ја̏ре with ја̏рац - that is an adult billy goat.

The universal word is младу́нче: младунче лава - a lion cub.
title: Baby animals

note:
Serbian cakes have telling names:
• Срнећа леђа - a walnut sponge with chocolate glaze
• Мо̏сква шни̏т - the signature of the hotel «Москва»: vanilla cream, cherry, pineapple and almonds
• Васина торта - walnuts, orange and chocolate; by legend the recipe was invented by the mother-in-law of a man named Vasa from Параћин
• Реформ торта - chocolate and walnut; the name is linked to the socialist reforms in Yugoslavia
title: Names of Serbian cakes

note:
Слага̀лица is a beloved Serbian TV quiz show, based on the French show "Des chiffres et des lettres". It has eight rounds.

The host Milka Canić always opened simply: До̀бро ве̏че̄! - everyone knows this phrase.

There is also a morning counterpart: Бео̀граде, до̀бро ју̏тро. It was the name of a program by the writer and journalist Duško Radović, which aired on «Студио Б» in 1975-1982.
title: "Слагалица" and "Добро вече"

note:
In гледање у шољу people look at the shapes the та́лог left at the bottom of the cup.

Birds:
• го̏лӯб - good luck
• ла̏бӯд - success
• ла́ста - don't rush decisions
• о̀рао - a change for the better
• га̏вра̄н - bad news
• гу̏ска - you will find a solution

Animals:
• ма̏чка - a quarrel and deceit
• па̏с - a faithful friend
• о́вца - happiness
• пра̑се - temptation and prosperity
• ко̏њ - good income
• зе̑ц - speed or shame

Elements: во̀да - money, ва̏тра - be careful.
title: What the shapes in coffee grounds mean

related.en: a word with the root чест
old word for a water source
"black one" (monks were called so for their clothes)

note:
Many ordinary words came from Turkish and displaced Slavic ones:
• ка̀пија - replaced вратнице (wicker gates)
• са̀пӯн - replaced ми̏ло (from ми̏ти, "to wash", compare уми́вати)
• ча́мац - replaced чу̑н
• пѐшкӣр - replaced ру̀чнӣк and о̏тарак
• па́рче and ко̀ма̄д - replaced the old че̑ст, which survives in чѐшња̄к and причестити се
• ђу̏бре - took the place of гно̑ј
• бу̀на̄р - replaced студе́нац and кла̏денац
• че̏сма - took the place of то̏чка

Мо̀нах and ка̀луђер both come from Greek: they named the people who used to be called цр̀нац because of their black clothes.
title: Native words and Turkisms: who was displaced

related.en: Baš Čelik, a Serbian folk villain

note:
Ба̏ш-Чѐлик ("steel head" in Turkish) is a character of folk tales: a very strong, almost invulnerable giant who kidnaps beautiful girls.

Некрштенци are souls of children who died unbaptized: at night they fly as birds and drink the milk of cows and sheep.

A вукодлак can be an unborn child of a pregnant woman who died, if an animal runs over the grave.

Псоглавци are creatures with a human body and a dog's head.

Ба̏бица used to mean "midwife"; now it means an obstetric nurse.
title: Serbian folklore creatures: Baš Čelik and others

note:
Betting shops are on every corner in Serbia, so the betting vocabulary comes in handy.

Cards: карте in a шпил are де̑ле (dealt) and мешају (shuffled). Коцкице бацају - dice are thrown.

Bets:
• у́лог - a stake in a game
• о̏пклада - a wager
• кво́та - the bookmaker's odds

Results: доби́так - winnings, губи́так - a loss.

Cards by value: десетка, дѐве̄тка, осмица, сѐдмица, шестица. Блефи́рати - to bluff.
title: Cards, dice and bets

related.en: to smack one's lips, to chew noisily

note:
Verbs of the body and not-so-elegant habits.

Sounds and physiology: хр́кати, шту̏цати, подриги́вати, ка̀шљати, ки́јати, зно̀јити се.

Nose: ду́вати но̑с, шмр̀цати, ча̏чкати но̑с.

Mouth: пљу̏вати, мља̏цкати, ба̏лавити.

Other: гри̏сти но̏кте, цедити бубуљице, пр́љати.
title: Verbs of the body and not-so-elegant habits

note:
The Balkans have exchanged words for centuries, and part of the everyday vocabulary came from Greek. Many words sound almost the same as their Greek counterparts: ти̏гањ, тр̀пеза, ха̀ртија, крѐвет, лѝвада.

Through the church came ѝкона and ма̏настӣр.

From the kitchen and home: бѝбер, сто̏ма̄к - not the organ, but the belly.
title: Greek words in Serbian

note:
The word ре̑д covers order, queue, row and layer at once. This gives a whole family:
• по̏ред
• ре̏досле̄д
• др̏воре̄д
• уре́дити
• преуредити - including rearranging furniture

So "Lady in red" sounds to a Serb like "a lady in order" (дама у реду): red in Serbian is цр̀вен.
title: The root red: order, row, queue

related.en: to entertain, to get a crowd going

note:
Serbian verbs in -ирати and -овати look international, and most are easy to guess from English; note аними́рати, which is mostly about entertaining a crowd:
• ирити́рати - to irritate
• прецизирати - to specify, to clarify
• неги́рати - to deny
• аними́рати - to entertain and get a crowd going
• едуковати - to train, to educate
• ко̀мпликовати - to complicate
• инсисти́рати - to insist

Verbs in -ирати conjugate like -ам verbs: прецизирам. Verbs in -овати give -ујем: едукујем, компликујем. Most are biaspectual.
title: Verbs that look international

related.en: the wedding best man, the witness
the old kum, a kum across generations

note:
Ку́мство is a close bond between families, often almost like kinship.

Ку̑м can be the witness at a wedding (венчани кум) or a godfather (крштени кум). Стари кум is the one whose family has been friends with yours for generations.

The sons of kums often become kums to each other too. A kum is a friend who was chosen into the family.
title: Кум: more than a "best man"

related.en: how are you doing, where have you been

note:
A neutral phrase often has a more relaxed counterpart:
• не брини - ла̏гано, бре̏
• морам да идем - одох
• обична ствар - ништа спец
• ка̏ко си - где̏ си

This sounds friendly. Don't answer strangers and older people this way.
title: Textbook and street Serbian

related.en: the Latin name of Novi Sad

note:
The city is abbreviated НС.

The historic nickname is Српска Атина. The Latin name is Неопланта, the Hungarian one is Újvidék.

On declension see the grammar: both parts of Нови Сад decline in Serbian.
title: Other names for Novi Sad

note:
Врбица, or Лазарева субота, is a children's holiday on the eve of Palm Sunday (Цвети).

Mothers dress the children up, put венчићи on their heads and hang звончићи on a tricolor ribbon around their necks.

In church young willow branches are blessed and then kept at home by the icon.
title: Врбица: Lazarus Saturday

note:
A playful "dictionary of sounds":
• «а» - I didn't catch that
• «е̏» - oh, come on, you're kidding
• «и» - what's so strange about it
• «о» - well, that's news
• уф - scary
• у̏х - awkward, unpleasant
• ех - it used to be like that, now it's only talked about
• ах - a missed chance
• их - if only I had known
• па - so what?
• ма̏ - never mind, forget it
title: What the interjections say

note:
The Russian TV series "The Boy's Word" was shown in Serbia under the title Часна уличарска - literally "honest street".

The title plays on the expression часна реч - "word of honor". It is a translation by meaning, not a literal one.
title: "The Boy's Word" in Serbian

related.sr: До̏бар да̑н, Ма̀рија је на телѐфону.
related.en: Good afternoon, this is Marija (literally "Marija is on the phone").

note:
People pick up the phone with Ха̏ло! or Мо̏лим!, or politely with Изволите?.

The caller introduces themselves in the third person: Добар дан, Марија је на телефону.

To ask for someone: Могу ли да добијем Стефана?

The reason for the call is stated right away: Зовем у вези са огласом.

Calls end with Ва́жи, Договорено, Чу̏је̄мо се, А̀јде, здра̏во.

If you can't get through: Зовем, нико се не јавља.
title: A phone call in Serbian

note:
Слага̀лица is the best-known quiz on Serbian public TV.

In one of the rounds (спојнице) you have to connect pairs: dog breeds and cartoon characters, republics and their capitals.

The philologist Милка Цанић (1944-2016), the quiz's editor and proofreader, stayed in viewers' memory with her greeting До̀бро ве̏че̄!. Say her name to a Serb and he will most likely answer with exactly that.
title: "Слагалица": a Serbian TV quiz

note:
Basic directions: пра́во, де̏сно, ле̑во, на̏пре̄д, на̏за̄д, го̏ре, до̏ле.

Behind the wheel: рикверц - reverse gear, у рикверц - in reverse.

About movement: цикцак, укруг.

Turned over: на̏опачке̄, наглава̀чке̄.

Watch out: пра́во means "straight ahead", not "right". "Right" is де̏сно.
title: Where to drive, where to go: direction words

note:
The names of the planets are close to the English ones: Мѐркӯр, Вѐнера, Зѐмља, Ма̏рс, Ју̀питер, Са̀турн, У̀ра̄н, Нѐптӯн, Плу̀то̄н. Only Earth is different: Зѐмља.

The Sun is Су̑нце, the Moon is Ме̏се̄ц, and "star" is зве́зда.
title: Planets in Serbian

note:
Astronomy words: celestial bodies, phenomena and equipment.

Celestial bodies: коме́та, астеро̀ӣд, метѐо̄р, звезда падалица, суперно̑ва, црна рупа.

Phenomena and equipment: о̏рбита, те̏лескоп, све̏мӣрскӣ бро̑д, међузвездана прашина.

"Space" is usually све̏мӣр, and the whole Universe is Унивѐрзум.

An eclipse is помра̀че̄ње: помрачење Сунца, and a lunar eclipse is помрачење Месеца.
title: Space and astronomy

note:
Words found in news and appeals for help: Црвени крст, волонтер, ѝзбеглица, жр̏тва, хуманитарна помоћ, спасилачка операција, евакуа́ција, рехабилита́ција, психолошка подршка, прихватни центар.

Two phrases that both can be rendered as "emergency help":
• хитна помоћ - the ambulance service and its call-out
• прва помоћ - first aid given on the spot before doctors arrive
title: The Red Cross and aid: vocabulary

note:
Breed names are mostly borrowed but spelled by Serbian rules: чивава, мопс, булдог, лабрадор, златни ретривер.

Јазавѝчар (dachshund) comes from ја̏завац ("badger"). A German shepherd is нѐмачкӣ о̀вча̄р, a poodle is пу̏дла or пу̀длица.
title: Dog breeds in Serbian

related.en: the Serbian New Year, January 13 (Orthodox calendar)

note:
Serbia sees in the New Year from December 31 to January 1, and on January 13 it also celebrates the Orthodox one - Српска Нова година.

People usually celebrate at home. The table has руска салата, са̀рма, various meats, колачи and ра̀кија.

Young people gather at friends' places or go to a concert. At midnight they congratulate each other and watch the ва̏троме̄т.

On holidays people like to watch old TV series such as Сре̏ћнӣ љу̑ди.
title: New Year in Serbia: the table and two holidays

note:
In one legend people carried darkness out of their house in buckets because it was dark inside. Saint Sava taught them to cut windows (про́зор), and they were very grateful.

In another, a disciple's honey (ме̑д) went missing. Sava said loudly that a bee (пчѐла) would land on the thief's (ло́пов) hat that day. The thief feared it all day and gave himself away.
title: Two legends about Saint Sava

note:
Signs often use short imperative forms:
• Вуци and Гурај - "pull" and "push" on doors
• Не гази траву
• Не дирај

The rest are nouns or participles:
• Забра̏њен у̀лаз, Забрањено паркирање
• Тишѝна
• Пажња, клизаво!, Па̀жња, стѐпенице!
• Чувај се пса
• Вѝсок на́пон
title: Signs and notices in the street

related.en: it was heard at the market

note:
For Serbs a пѝјаца is not just a market but a place with character: on Каленићева and Бајлонијева пијаца and at Зелени венац a person feels at home.

Каленићева пијаца opened in 1926 on land bequeathed to the city by the patron Влајко Каленић. The writer Момо Капор called it an exhibition of living still lifes.

Market words: тѐзга, гајбица, кило и по.

The expression чуло се на пијаци meant: it was heard at the market, i.e. the information is reliable even though the newspapers are silent.
title: A Belgrade market: Каленић and others

note:
Four Serbian painters:
• Паја Јовановић - the main realist, author of Кићење невесте: bridesmaids in folk costumes dress the bride for the wedding
• Надежда Петровић brought impressionism and expressionism to early 20th-century Serbia (Ко̏сово по̏ље)
• Сава Шумановић studied in Paris and combined cubism with the landscapes of Srem (Шидијанке)
• Милена Павловић-Барили, close to surrealism, worked in New York: her drawing made the cover of Vogue in April 1940

Words for talking about painting: сли̏ка̄р, пла́тно, пѐјза̄ж, потез четкицом, јарке боје.
title: Four Serbian painters

related.en: I'm in front of the building.
The intercom doesn't work, I'll let you in.
Can you leave it with a neighbor?

note:
To pick up a parcel is подићи пошиљку; a notice of arrival, извештај о приспећу, is left in the mailbox. Also useful: бро̑ј за пра̏ће̄ње, пакомат.

The courier calls:
• Ево ме испред зграде
• Има ли ко да сиђе?
• Имате откупнину

Replies:
• Силазим одмах
• Не ради интерфон, отворићу вам
• Можете ли оставити код комшије?
• Имате ли ситно? - Ѝма̄м са̏мо кру̏пно

To pay on delivery is платити поузећем.
title: Couriers and parcels: words and phrases

note:
At the first football World Cup in Uruguay (1930) the Yugoslav team reached the semifinal, beating Brazil.

The cult film Монтевидео, бог те видео! was made about this trip, about ordinary Belgrade guys: the cobbler Tirke and the society man Moša.

The title plays on a rhyme: Монтевидео - "God saw you".

Football words: у̀такмица, навѝја̄ч, шутѝрати.
title: Монтевидео, бог те видео!
